en.s1: Both start at the same height and reach the same destination. Ignoring differences in efficiency, the change in gravitational potential energy of the load is the same in both cases.
en.s2: There is a difference: one elevator completes the trip in 10 seconds, while the other takes 30 seconds.

en.s47: Power makes it possible to compare how rapidly very different systems transfer or transform energy.
en.s48: An LED can operate on a few watts. A household appliance can require hundreds or thousands of watts. An industrial motor can operate at the scale of kilowatts or megawatts, while large generating units reach even greater scales.

en.s52: A power plant therefore has installed power expressed in MW, while energy generated over a given period can be expressed in MWh or GWh. The first measure indicates the generation rate; the second, the amount generated during the interval.
en.s54: More powerful equipment is not necessarily more efficient.
en.s56: describes a rate of energy transfer or transformation.
en.s58: compares how much of the energy supplied to a system results in the effect considered useful.
en.s59: Two motors can provide the same mechanical output power and have different efficiencies. The less efficient one will need more energy to achieve the same useful result.

en.s67: A reservoir can store a large amount of potential energy and release it slowly. Another system can have less available energy, but transfer it rapidly and develop high power over a short interval.
en.s68: Knowing only the available energy does not fully describe how a system behaves. We also need to know how quickly that energy can be transferred or transformed.
en.s70: Power measures the speed of an energy transfer or transformation.
en.s71: One watt equals one joule per second.
en.s72: Kilowatt is a unit of power; kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy.
en.s73: Energy use depends on both power and operating time.
en.s74: Greater power does not, by itself, mean greater efficiency.
